description: We are team BunBo_KoHanh from Ho Chi Minh City! Our goal is to build an engaging, retro-styled web strategy game where players step into the shoes of a NASA Flight Director—making tough mission design trade-offs, managing budgets, and handling space crises. We're looking for passionate teammates with skills in UI/UX design, creative storytelling, or space science to join us and bring this interactive experience to life!
summary:
ABANDONN is an interactive educational space mission design game inspired by The Martian and grounded in real NASA systems-engineering frameworks. Combining comic-style storytelling with hands-on simulation, the game challenges players to rescue a stranded astronaut across two interconnected phases.
         - In Phase 1, players manage power budgets under Martian dust storms (MEDA), operate MOXIE oxygen generation and ECLSS water recycling, and relay survival telemetry via the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter to Earth’s Deep Space Network. 
         - In Phase 2, players enter NASA’s Mission Design Lab to configure rockets, propulsion, power systems (Solar vs. RTG), trajectories, and crew rations—balancing real engineering trade-offs across mass, Delta , power, and communications margins before clearing a JPL Concept Maturity Level (CML 4) review and Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL).By translating complex aerospace constraints and post-mission failure analyses into intuitive gameplay, ABANDONN empowers students to experience how integrated mission teams solve high-stakes engineering problems.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO AND HOW DOES IT WORK?

ABANDONN is an interactive, two-phase space mission design and survival simulation game inspired by The Martian. Designed around NASA's four core mission segments (Launch, Space, Ground, and User/Science), the game places players on both sides of an interplanetary rescue operation, connecting surface survival on Mars with aerospace systems engineering at Earth Mission Control.

The experience begins with a wordless, hand-storyboarded graphic-novel prologue depicting the Horizon-IV crew evacuating during a violent Martian dust storm, accidentally leaving one astronaut behind. From there, gameplay unfolds across two synchronized phases linked by a dramatic 13-screen intermission comic when Earth receives the survivor's signal:

In Phase 1 (Mars Surface Survival and Orbital Relay), the player controls the stranded astronaut inside the Mars Hab. Using a point-and-click interface, players must ration limited electrical power affected by atmospheric dust opacity (modeled on Mars 2020 MEDA telemetry), balance oxygen generation via MOXIE carbon-dioxide electrolysis, maintain ECLSS water recycling, and manage physical stamina across Martian Sols. Because the Hab's primary high-gain dish is destroyed, players must tune a short-range UHF antenna to match the overhead orbital pass of the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), optimize signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and compress critical telemetry (coordinates, vitals, and remaining rations) within a strict byte limit to relay a distress packet to Earth's Deep Space Network (DSN).

In Phase 2 (NASA Mission Design Lab and Rescue Execution), the player transitions to Earth Mission Control. The actual survival data from Phase 1—including remaining Sols of food, water, and oxygen, as well as active weather conditions—automatically sets the deadline and environmental hazards for the rescue mission. Players enter an interactive Spacecraft Assembly Bay to configure six interconnected subsystems: Propulsion (launch vehicle), Propellant (delta-v capacity), Spacecraft Bus (Solar Panels versus RTG nuclear power, and Airbag versus Skycrane landing systems), Communications (X-Band versus Ka-Band dishes), Rescue Cargo and Crew Rations (sustaining a three-person rescue crew plus emergency supplies), and Interplanetary Trajectory (comparing fuel-efficient Hohmann transfers against high-energy Fast Transit paths on a live 2D Solar System map). Before launching, designs must pass a JPL Concept Maturity Level 4 (CML 4) safety review featuring four animated telemetry dial gauges enforcing at least 35% mass and power margins, alongside mandatory COSPAR Planetary Protection sterilization and RTG launch safety approvals. Once launched, players monitor the transit, transmit a DSN command to Mars (earth:dsn-command-sent), switch back to deploy a ground landing beacon (mars:beacon-deployed), and guide the spacecraft through Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) to unlock a 9-screen True Ending or one of eight diagnostic Failure Endings.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

Tangible Engineering Trade-Offs: Instead of abstract formulas, players directly observe how adding extra crew rations or heavier landing hardware increases dry mass, reduces delta-v braking capability under the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, and extends transit duration beyond the stranded astronaut's remaining survival Sols.

Integrated Onboarding and NASA Knowledge Hub: To prevent beginners from feeling overwhelmed by mission-control interfaces, ABANDONN combines a contextual first-time spotlight tutorial with an interactive Mission Log checklist that automatically strikes through completed objectives. Every spacecraft module also includes a Magnifying Glass inspector displaying deep technical specs alongside direct links to official NASA science and engineering articles.

Diagnostic Failure Analysis and Checkpoint Iteration: Rather than a generic Game Over screen, any failure—whether hypoxia, dust-storm power blackout, trajectory overshoot, crew cohesion collapse, or EDL crash—triggers an illustrated ending and a root-cause engineering report explaining what went wrong. Players can immediately reload from multi-slot automatic checkpoints to refine their design and test new hypotheses.

WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT?

Bridging Classroom Theory and Systems Engineering: High school and university students often learn orbital mechanics, thermodynamics, propulsion, or telecommunications as isolated subjects. ABANDONN demonstrates how these disciplines operate as a single, tightly coupled system where every engineering decision creates cascading consequences across cost, mass, power, and human survival.

Accessible, Inclusive STEM Outreach: By pairing emotional, easy-to-follow visual storytelling with full bilingual support (English and Vietnamese) and plain-language explanations of real aerospace standards, the project lowers the entry barrier for students worldwide to explore space mission architecture and human spaceflight operations.

WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, AND SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

Languages and Web Architecture: Built with HTML5, CSS3 (custom tactical glassmorphism HUD, responsive arc gauges, and keyframe animations), and modular Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+). All physics calculations are centralized in a decoupled simulation engine (phase2-engine.js) synchronized with Phase 1 via a custom event-driven state bridge (CustomEvent and localStorage checkpoint manager) hosted locally through VS Code Live Server.

Interactive Graphics and Visualization: HTML5 Canvas and layered SVG graphics power real-time Solar System orbital plotting, dynamic dust-storm particle physics, layered spacecraft blueprint assembly, and telemetry gauges.

Scientific Data and Frameworks: Grounded in NASA's Design and Develop Science Missions handbook, JPL Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1-4), Goddard Mission Design Lab (MDL) trade-study workflows, General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) trajectory principles, NASA Mission Viz concepts, Mars 2020 (MOXIE and MEDA) instrument telemetry, NASA Veggie and BioNutrients research, and COSPAR Planetary Protection guidelines.

Hardware and Development Workflow: Developed on an HP Victus 16 workstation and a digital tablet used to hand-draw all comic storyboards and UI wireframes. Software tools included Cursor IDE, VS Code, Git and GitHub for version control, AI-assisted comic illustration workflows, custom Python scripts (PIL and rembg) for clean transparent sprite extraction, and Playwright for automated headless browser verification.

HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

Synchronized Dual-Perspective Gameplay: Rather than treating surface survival and spacecraft engineering as separate mini-games, ABANDONN couples them into one continuous narrative loop where the player's own survival efficiency in Phase 1 directly dictates the rescue window and environmental risks in Phase 2.

Minimum Compliance Versus Mission Robustness: Passing the CML 4 safety review at the 80% green threshold unlocks the launchpad, but borderline yellow margins or mismatched hardware—such as relying on Solar Panels during an active Martian dust storm—can still cause realistic mid-flight or landing failures. This teaches players the crucial aerospace distinction between meeting minimum launch rules and engineering a truly resilient mission.

Wordless Visual Storytelling with Layered Motion: Hand-crafted comic panels combined with parallax backgrounds, breathing character animations, and real-time environmental particle effects convey high-stakes emergencies intuitively across languages without relying on walls of text.

WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

Scientific Realism Versus Accessibility: We deliberately avoided common sci-fi inaccuracies—such as growing crops directly in toxic perchlorate-laden Martian soil or instantaneous Earth-Mars voice calls—and replaced them with authentic physics including light-time communication delays, UHF orbiter relays, and safety margin engineering, while translating technical jargon into approachable tooltips.

Cognitive Load and Player Guidance: Recognizing that complex mission-design dashboards can intimidate first-time players, we embedded step-by-step guidance directly into the Mission Log checklist and highlighted interactive controls progressively.

Intellectual Property and Safety Compliance: All mission branding (Horizon-IV), character designs, and visual assets were originally created for this project without using restricted agency logos or trademarks.
